lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 science you met tectonic plates. About how fast do they move? (A few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.) Today: what happens where plates meet, and why people live there.

Earth has layers: a thin rocky crust, about 7 km thick under the oceans and 35 km under the continents; the hot mantle, which flows very slowly; and a metal core. The crust is cracked into about seven large and many smaller tectonic plates.

Where plates move apart (a divergent, or constructive, boundary), magma rises and makes new crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs down the Atlantic, which widens about 2.5 cm a year; Iceland sits on top of it, with volcanoes and hot springs.

Where an ocean plate meets a continent (a destructive boundary), the heavier ocean plate sinks beneath it into the mantle. A deep trench forms, and melting rock rises to make volcanoes, as in the Andes and Japan. The biggest earthquakes happen here.

Where two continents collide, neither sinks, so the crust crumples upwards into fold mountains. India is still pushing into Asia, about 5 cm a year. So the Himalayas are still rising, by a few millimetres a year.

Where plates slide past (a conservative boundary), no crust is made or lost, but they stick and jerk: earthquakes, as on California's San Andreas Fault. Each whole step up the magnitude scale is 10 times the shaking and about 32 times the energy.

Why live near danger? Volcanic ash makes rich soil for farms; hot rocks give geothermal energy, about a quarter of Iceland's electricity and most of its heating; volcanoes bring tourists and minerals; and many families have lived there for generations.

Try it in the world: build a cross-section of a plate boundary in blocks: two plates, a trench, a volcano and its magma. Put an arrow sign on each plate showing which way it moves. Next: rocks, weathering and soils.

exercises.prompt: Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
exercises.hint: It is the thin outer skin.
exercises.explain: The crust: thin and rocky, about 7 km under oceans and 35 km under continents.

exercises.prompt: What forms where two plates move apart?
exercises.explain: Magma rises into the gap and cools into new crust.

exercises.prompt: The Himalayas formed where two continental plates collided.
exercises.explain: True: neither plate sank, so the crust crumpled up into fold mountains.

exercises.prompt: Which boundary runs down the middle of the Atlantic?
exercises.hint: Iceland sits on top of it.
exercises.explain: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates move apart.

exercises.prompt: Why do many people farm near volcanoes?
exercises.hint: What does ash add to the soil?
exercises.explain: Volcanic ash is full of minerals, so the soil is rich for crops.

exercises.prompt: Sort these by how the plates move.
items: the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
exercises.hint: New crust: apart. Trenches and mountains: together. Torn sideways: sliding past.
exercises.explain: Apart: Iceland, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Together: the Andes, the Himalayas. Sliding past: the San Andreas and Alpine Faults.

exercises.prompt: The Atlantic widens about 2.5 cm a year. How many cm does it widen in 100 years?
exercises.hint: Multiply the cm a year by the years.

exercises.prompt: Where an ocean plate meets a continent, which plate sinks?
exercises.hint: Ocean crust is heavier for its size.
exercises.explain: The heavier ocean plate sinks under the continent.

exercises.prompt: Match each boundary to what its plates do.
exercises.hint: Diverge means go different ways; converge means come together.
exercises.explain: Divergent: apart. Convergent: together. Transform: sliding past. Subduction: one plate sinks under the other.

exercises.hint: It is the deep dip where one plate goes down.
exercises.explain: A deep ocean trench, where the ocean plate sinks.

exercises.prompt: How many times more ground shaking does a magnitude 7 earthquake cause than a magnitude 5 one?
exercises.hint: Each whole step is 10 times the shaking.

exercises.prompt: Why are there no volcanoes along the San Andreas Fault?
exercises.hint: Where does the magma for volcanoes come from at a destructive boundary?
choices: no plate is sinking and melting there
exercises.explain: The plates slide past each other, so no plate sinks and melts to make magma.

exercises.prompt: New crust is made where plates slide past each other.
exercises.hint: Is crust made, lost, or neither at a transform boundary?
exercises.explain: False: at a transform (conservative) boundary no crust is made or lost.

exercises.prompt: India moves about 5 cm a year into Asia. How many km is that in 1 million years? (100,000 cm = 1 km.)
exercises.hint: Find the cm in a million years, then turn cm into km.

exercises.prompt: How does Iceland use its plate boundary?
exercises.hint: What heats the water in its hot springs?
choices: hot rocks give geothermal heat and power
it builds ski slopes on lava
exercises.explain: Hot rocks near the surface heat water: geothermal energy heats most homes and makes about a quarter of the electricity.
